title: Macroeconomic Equilibrium
page_title: Macroeconomic equilibrium - CIE A Level Economics

blocks.md: - Real national output equilibrium occurs where **aggregate demand** (AD) intersects with **short-run aggregate supply **(SRAS)

blocks.alt: Graph showing AD and SRAS curves intersecting. Y-axis: Average Price Level (£), X-axis: Real GDP. Intersection labelled AP₁ and Y₁.
blocks.caption: A diagram showing short-run equilibrium in an economy at an equilibrium price level of AP1 and real output of Y1

blocks.md:
- This economy is in **short run equilibrium** at AP<sub>1</sub>Y<sub>1</sub>
- Any changes to the components of AD will cause the AD curve to shift left or right, creating a** new short-run equilibrium**
- Any changes to the determinants of SRAS will shift the SRAS curve left or right, creating a** new short-run equilibrium**
- The level of **employment** in the economy is determined by the equilibrium level of output - at Y1, firms require a corresponding level of workers to produce that output

  - If equilibrium output rises, employment rises; if equilibrium output falls, employment falls

- **Free market economists** believe that the economy will **always return to its normal capacity level of output**

  - In the short-run, there will be fluctuations around this capacity level of output
  - In the long-run, the economy will return to this normal capacity level of output, but perhaps at a different **average price level**
- It is important to understand the long-run macroeconomic equilibrium as it is used to identify ***positive*** and ***negative*** output gaps in an economy (this is covered in more detail later on)

blocks.alt: Graph of long-run aggregate supply (LRAS), short-run aggregate supply (SRAS), and aggregate demand (AD) with axes for average price level and real GDP.
blocks.caption: A diagram that shows the free market view of long-run equilibrium which occurs at the intersection of long-run aggregate supply (LRAS), short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) & aggregate demand (AD)

blocks.md:
- The **LRAS **curve demonstrates the **normal capacity level of output** of the economy using all of its **scarce resources**
- The **SRAS intersects with AD **at the LRAS curve
- This economy is producing at the **full employment level **of output (Y<sub>FE</sub>)
- The **average price level **at Y<sub>FE </sub>is AP<sub>1</sub>

- The Keynesian view challenges the classical assumption that the economy will always return to full employment output
- **In the Keynesian model, the economy can settle in long-run equilibrium below full employment** - where AD intersects the elastic section of the Keynesian LRAS

  - At this point, there is significant spare capacity and unemployment in the economy
  - The price level is stable because spare resources can be brought into production without bidding up *factor prices*
  - The economy will not automatically self-correct - without government intervention it may remain at this low output equilibrium indefinitely

blocks.alt: Graph showing long-run aggregate supply with average price level and real GDP axes. AD curve shifts right from AD1 to AD2, lowering price from P1 to P2.

blocks.md:
- The economy is initially in equilibrium at P<sub>1</sub>Y<sub>FE </sub>- at the full employment level of output on the vertical section of the Keynesian LRAS

  - A fall in AD causes the AD curve to shift left from AD<sub>1 </sub>to AD<sub>2</sub>
  - The new equilibrium is at P<sub>2</sub>Y<sub>1</sub> - below the full employment level of output Y<sub>FE</sub>
  - There is now a **negative output gap** equal to Y<sub>1</sub>Y<sub>FE</sub> - the economy is producing below its potential
- The price level has fallen from P<sub>1 </sub>to P<sub>2</sub> - the economy is on the upward-sloping section of the Keynesian LRAS where both output and price level changes occur
- Unlike the classical model, **the economy will not automatically return to Y**<sub>**FE**</sub> - wages and prices are sticky downwards and the self-correction mechanism breaks down at low levels of output
- This provides the Keynesian justification for **government intervention** - an increase in AD via *expansionary fiscal policy* can shift AD<sub>2</sub> back rightward, raising output and employment back towards Y<sub>FE</sub>

blocks.alt: Economic graph shows aggregate demand and supply curves, with LRAS, SRAS, AD, AD1, price levels AP1, AP2, and GDP levels Y1, Y2, YFE marked.
blocks.caption: An increase in aggregate demand

blocks.md:
- The **initial equilibrium** level of output was at **AP**<sub>**1**</sub>**Y**<sub>**1**</sub>
- An** increase **in one of the components of ***AD*** (e.g. consumption) causes the AD to **increase AD**<sub>**1**</sub>**→AD**<sub>**2**</sub>
- **Average prices** in the economy rise to **AP**<sub>**2**</sub> and the real level of **output increases to Y**<sub>**2**</sub>
- The new **short-run equilibrium** is at AP<sub>2</sub>Y<sub>2</sub>
- As output rises from Y<sub>1</sub> to Y<sub>2</sub>, firms require more workers to meet higher demand - **employment rises**; conversely a fall in AD would reduce output and employment

blocks.text: 2. An increase in short run aggregate supply (SRAS)

blocks.alt: Economic graph showing shifts in Short-Run Aggregate Supply (SRAS) from SRAS1 to SRAS2, affecting average price level (AP1 to AP2) and real GDP (Y1 to Y2).
blocks.caption: An increase in the short-run aggregate supply (SRAS) causes higher outputs and lower prices

blocks.md:
- The **initial equilibrium** level of output was at **AP**<sub>**1**</sub>**Y**<sub>**1**</sub>

  - This equilibrium represents a** **negative output gap equal to **Y**<sub>**1**</sub>**Y**<sub>**FE**</sub>
- An** increase **in one of the determinants of ***SRAS*** (e.g. productivity) causes the SRAS to **increase SRAS**<sub>**1**</sub>**→SRAS**<sub>**2**</sub>
- **Average prices** in the economy fall to **AP**<sub>**2**</sub> and the real level of **output increases to Y**<sub>**2**</sub>
- The new **short-run equilibrium** is at **AP**<sub>**2**</sub>**Y**<sub>**2**</sub>
- There is still a **negative output gap** but it is smaller **(Y**<sub>**2**</sub>**Y**<sub>**FE**</sub>**)**
- As output rises from Y<sub>1</sub> to Y<sub>2</sub>, more workers are needed in production - **employment rises** and the negative output gap narrows, meaning unemployment falls though it does not return to zero until YFE is reached

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
A government has increased output with no effect on the price level.

![Graph showing Aggregate Supply (AS) curve intersecting with four Aggregate Demand (AD) curves labelled AD1 to AD4, indicating price level and output.](assets/0ea13965030c-47129-29-worked-example.png)

**What must have been the initial level of aggregate demand?**

A. AD<sub>1</sub>    B. AD<sub>2</sub>    C. AD<sub>3 </sub>   D. AD<sub>4</sub>

**Final answer:** **Answer: A - AD1**

**Worked solution**

This question tests understanding of the Keynesian LRAS and which section of the curve the economy is operating on.

The key condition in the question is that output increased **with no effect on the price level**. This can only occur on the **highly elastic (flat) section** of the Keynesian LRAS - where there is significant spare capacity and unemployment, so firms can increase output by drawing on idle resources without bidding up factor prices.

- If AD shifts right from a position on the elastic section, real output rises, but the price level remains unchanged
- If the economy were already on the upward-sloping or vertical section, any rightward shift in AD would raise the price level

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
Always state the effect on **all three variables** when analysing an AD or AS shift - real output, the price level, and employment.

A common error is to identify the new equilibrium price and output but forget employment entirely. Remember that employment moves in the same direction as real output - rising output means firms need more workers; falling output means fewer workers are needed.

For the Keynesian model, always identify which section of the LRAS the economy is operating on before analysing the effect of an AD shift. A rightward shift in AD on the elastic section raises output without raising prices and increases employment - the same shift on the vertical section is purely inflationary with no output or employment effect.
